newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Currency board may boost Bulgaria investment - EBRD.
newsitem.headline: Currency board may boost Bulgaria investment - EBRD.

text.p: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) said on Thursday a currency board would improve the climate for investment in Bulgaria only if combined with speedy structural reform.

"Stability achieved by whatever means, be that a currency board or another measure, will only be lasting if combined with a very strong structural reform," EBRD senior economist Hans Peter Lankes told a news conference.
"We are certain a greater stability will be instrumental for investment programmes like ours to go forward," he added.
The EBRD has revised its funding strategy for Bulgaria, saying delayed reforms had deterred development of the private sector.
"Delays of structural reforms, primarily at the enterprise level, have been the source of Bulgaria's current currency crisis," said Lankes.
The lev has plummeted from 70 to the dollar at the beginning of this year to an all-time law of 395 a week ago. It traded on Thursday at around 355 to the dollar.

Bulgaria will fail to meet the EBRD's requirement for members to reach a 60/40 private/public investment portfolio distribution by June 1997, five years after the EBRD began operations to help the transition to a market economy in central and eastern Europe.
The EBRD has approved 21 investment projects in Bulgaria totalling over 210 million European Currency Units (Ecu).
Only 20 percent of these investments are committed to the private sector, EBRD Bulgaria Country Team Director Olivier Descamps told the same news conference.
"Once the macroeconomy stabilises we certainly could see ourselves investing in some of the large transactions that have been announced," said Descamps.

Desperate to raise cash for current expenses and debt payments, the government offered for sale two months ago some 20 major state firms, including 60 percent of soda ash producer Sodi Devnya, a 25 percent stake in Bulgarian Telecommunication Company (BTC), chemical firm Chimko and half a dozen cement plants.
Descamps said the EBRD was planning to invest in equity after the privatisation of these firms, when they would have a foreign management which would provide a viable business plan.

"They are good businesses. They have good export markets, and with some foreign management and upgraded equipment they would become the kind of businesses we would feel comfortable investing in," said Descamps.
The EBRD was also interested in investing in energy, pharmaceuticals and light industry, he added.
